name: Canjeero (Laxoox Pancakes)
description: Soft, spongy Somali pancakes with a honeycomb of tiny holes, served warm with butter and sugar or sesame oil and tea.
steps: In a large bowl, mix the plain flour, semolina, yeast, 2 tablespoons of the sugar, baking powder and salt.
Pour in the warm water gradually, whisking until you have a smooth, thin batter like single cream.
Cover the bowl with a clean towel and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until the batter is bubbly and has risen slightly.
Heat a non-stick frying pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil on kitchen paper.
Pour in a ladle of batter and tilt the pan to spread it into a thin circle. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes without flipping, until the top is dry and covered in small holes.
Slide the canjeero onto a plate and repeat with the remaining batter, re-oiling the pan lightly every few pancakes.
Serve warm, brushed with melted butter and sprinkled with the remaining 1 tablespoon sugar, with sweet tea on the side.
tips: Only cook one side. Flipping a canjeero ruins the holey top.
If the batter thickens as it sits, whisk in a splash of water.
photo: A stack of pale golden pancakes with a honeycomb of tiny holes on a white plate, one folded over to show the spongy texture, melted butter glistening and a dusting of sugar. A small glass of tea sits beside the plate.

name: Akara (Bean Fritters)
description: Crisp-edged, fluffy fritters made from whipped black-eyed bean paste, a classic Nigerian breakfast eaten with pap or bread.
steps: Soak the black-eyed beans in plenty of cold water for 15 minutes, then rub them between your hands to loosen the skins. Rinse repeatedly, pouring off the floating skins, until most are gone.
Roughly chop the onion, scotch bonnet and red pepper and place them in a blender with the peeled beans and 100 ml cold water.
Blend until you have a thick, smooth paste, adding a splash more water only if the blender struggles.
Transfer the paste to a bowl, add the salt and whisk vigorously with a wooden spoon for 3 to 5 minutes until the batter is light, fluffy and slightly paler.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep, heavy pan over medium-high heat until a drop of batter sizzles and rises straight away, about 180C.
Scoop heaped tablespoons of batter into the hot oil, a few at a time, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown.
Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain on kitchen paper and serve hot.
tips: Whisking adds air, which makes the fritters light instead of dense.
Fry in small batches so the oil temperature stays steady.
photo: A heap of round, deep golden-brown bean fritters with craggy crisp surfaces on a paper-lined plate, one broken open to reveal a pale fluffy interior. A small bowl of pepper sauce sits alongside.

name: Swahili Chapati
description: Soft, flaky, layered flatbreads rolled and coiled before frying, the East African way to scoop up stews or dunk in sweet chai. Makes 6 chapatis.
steps: Mix the plain flour, salt and sugar in a large bowl, then add 2 tablespoons of the oil and rub it in with your fingers.
Add the warm water a little at a time and knead for 10 minutes into a soft, smooth, slightly sticky dough.
Cover the dough with a damp cloth and rest it for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 6 balls. Roll one out thinly into a large circle, brush with oil, then roll it up like a sausage and coil the rope into a snail shape. Repeat with the rest and let the coils rest for 15 minutes.
Roll each coil out flat into a circle about 3 mm thick.
Heat a dry frying pan over medium heat. Cook one chapati for 1 minute until small bubbles form, flip, and brush the cooked side with a teaspoon of oil.
Flip again, oil the other side, and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more, pressing gently, until golden with brown spots. Keep the cooked chapatis wrapped in a towel while you cook the rest.
tips: Coiling the dough is what creates the flaky layers, so do not skip it.
Keep the chapatis wrapped in foil or a towel so they stay soft.
photo: A stack of round golden chapatis with brown blistered spots, the top one torn open to show soft flaky layers, on a wooden board with a cup of spiced chai beside it.

name: Misir Wat (Spiced Red Lentils)
description: A deep red, richly spiced Ethiopian lentil stew slow-cooked with berbere and plenty of onion, scooped up with injera.
steps: Rinse the red lentils in a sieve under cold water until the water runs clear.
Finely chop the onions. Place them in a large dry pot over medium heat and cook, stirring, for 8 minutes until softened and beginning to catch, without any fat yet.
Add the spiced clarified butter, grated garlic and ginger, and stir for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste and cook for 3 minutes, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Add the lentils and 900 ml water, bring to the boil, then reduce to low heat.
Simmer, partly covered, for 25 minutes, stirring often, until the lentils collapse into a thick stew. Add a little water if it gets too thick.
Season with salt and serve warm with injera or flatbread.
tips: Cooking the onions dry first is the traditional way and gives a deep, sweet base.
Use ghee with a pinch of cardamom and cumin if you cannot find niter kibbeh.
photo: A shallow bowl of thick, glossy brick-red lentil stew with a swirl of spiced butter on top, served beside folded spongy injera on a round platter.

name: Shiro (Chickpea Stew)
description: A silky, comforting stew of ground chickpea flour simmered with onion, garlic and berbere, an everyday Eritrean and Ethiopian favourite.
steps: Finely chop the onions and cook them in a pot with no oil over medium heat for 6 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.
Add the vegetable oil, chopped garlic and chopped tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until the tomatoes break down.
Stir in the berbere and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the water and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat.
Sprinkle in the shiro powder slowly with one hand while whisking constantly with the other, so no lumps form.
Reduce to low heat and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until thick, smooth and glossy. Add a splash of water if too thick.
Season with salt and serve hot with injera or flatbread.
tips: Sprinkle the powder in slowly while whisking to avoid lumps.
A spoonful of ghee stirred in at the end makes it richer.
photo: A bowl of smooth golden-orange chickpea stew with a shiny oil sheen and a pinch of chopped green chilli on top, placed on injera on a large round plate.

name: Moi Moi (Steamed Bean Pudding)
description: A soft, savoury steamed pudding of blended black-eyed beans, peppers and onion, studded with boiled egg and fish. Makes 6 portions.
steps: Soak the beans in cold water for 15 minutes, rub to remove the skins and rinse until mostly clean.
Hard-boil 3 of the eggs for 10 minutes, cool in cold water, peel and cut into quarters.
Blend the peeled beans with the peppers, onion and 300 ml warm water until completely smooth.
Pour into a bowl and stir in the oil, crumbled stock cube, ground crayfish and salt. Beat in the remaining raw egg.
Flake the drained mackerel into the batter and mix gently.
Pour the mixture into 6 oiled ramekins or heatproof cups, filling about three-quarters, and add a piece of boiled egg to each.

Cover each with foil. Place on a rack in a large pot with 3 cm of simmering water, cover the pot and steam over medium heat for 45 minutes until firm and a skewer comes out clean. Top up the water as needed.
tips: Smooth blending gives the silky texture. Blend longer if it looks grainy.
Leave out the fish and crayfish for a vegetarian version.
photo: Slices of firm, pale orange steamed bean pudding on a plate, one cut to reveal a wedge of boiled egg in the centre, served with a spoon of pap or bread alongside.

name: Waakye (Rice & Beans)
description: Ghana's beloved rice and black-eyed beans, tinted deep reddish-brown with millet leaf sheaths and served with boiled egg, gari, fried plantain and shito.
steps: Rinse the beans, place them in a large pot with the waakye leaves, baking soda and 1.5 litres water. Bring to the boil over high heat, then simmer on medium-low for 40 minutes until the beans are half cooked and the water is deep red-brown.
Rinse the rice in cold water until it runs clear.
Remove the leaves, add the rice and salt to the beans, stir and top up with water if needed so it sits about 2 cm above the rice.
Cover tightly and cook over low heat for 25 minutes until the rice is tender and has absorbed the liquid. Rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, hard-boil the eggs for 10 minutes, cool and peel them.
Slice the plantains diagonally and fry in the oil over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden and caramelised.
Serve the waakye with the eggs, plantain, gari and a spoonful of shito.
tips: If you cannot find waakye leaves, a few spoonfuls of dark tea and a pinch more baking soda give a similar colour, though less flavour.
The beans must be half cooked before the rice goes in, or they stay hard.
photo: A mound of deep reddish-brown rice and beans on a banana-leaf-lined plate, with halved boiled eggs, golden fried plantain slices, a scoop of gari and a spoonful of dark red shito sauce.

name: Sukuma Wiki with Ugali
description: Quick-sauteed collard greens with tomato and onion, served with firm, white maize-meal ugali. Kenya's everyday family meal.
steps: Strip the collard leaves from their thick stems, stack the leaves, roll them up and slice into thin ribbons. Wash well and drain.
Heat the oil in a large pan over medium heat and fry the sliced onion for 5 minutes until soft and golden.
Add the garlic and chopped tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes until they break down into a thick sauce. Stir in the ground coriander.
Add the greens in handfuls, turning until they wilt, then cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until tender but still bright green. Season with salt.
For the ugali, bring 600 ml of water to the boil in a heavy pot. Mix 100 g of the maize flour with 300 ml cold water and stir this into the boiling water to make a thin paste.
Cook for 3 minutes, then add the remaining maize flour in batches, mixing hard with a wooden spoon over low heat until it forms a stiff dough that pulls from the sides, about 5 minutes.
Cover and cook for 2 more minutes, then shape into a mound with the spoon. Serve slices of ugali with the greens.
tips: Do not overcook the greens or they turn dull and bitter.
Eat ugali with your right hand: pinch off a piece, roll it, make a dent and scoop up the greens.
photo: A smooth white dome of ugali next to a generous pile of glossy dark green sukuma wiki flecked with tomato, served on a simple enamel plate.

name: Bariis Iskukaris (Spiced Rice with Lamb)
description: Somalia's fragrant festive rice, cooked with lamb in a blend of cumin, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon and studded with raisins.
steps: Place the lamb in a pot with 700 ml water, 1 teaspoon salt and half the onion. Bring to the boil, skim, then simmer covered over low heat for 50 minutes until tender. Drain, keeping the stock.
Rinse the basmati rice until the water runs clear, then soak for 20 minutes and drain.
Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Fry the remaining sliced onions with the cinnamon stick and whole cloves for 8 minutes until golden.
Add the garlic and grated tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes. Stir in the cumin, coriander, cardamom and ground cinnamon and cook for 1 minute.
Add the lamb and fry for 3 minutes, then add the drained rice and stir for 1 minute.
Measure 650 ml of the lamb stock, adding water if needed, and pour it in with the grated carrot, raisins and remaining salt. Bring to the boil.
Cover tightly, reduce to the lowest heat and cook for 20 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes off the heat, fluff with a fork and serve with a banana on the side, as Somalis do, and a squeeze of lime.
tips: Soaking the rice keeps the grains long and separate.
Serve with sliced banana, a squeeze of lime and a spicy green sauce for the authentic Somali experience.
photo: A wide platter of fluffy golden-brown spiced rice dotted with raisins and grated carrot, topped with tender pieces of lamb, with a wedge of lime and a halved banana on the side.

name: Doro Wat (Chicken Stew)
description: Ethiopia's national dish: chicken slowly simmered in a rich berbere and onion sauce with spiced butter and hard-boiled eggs.
steps: Skin the chicken, score the pieces with a knife and rub with the lemon juice and half the salt. Leave for 15 minutes.
Finely chop the onions and cook them in a large heavy pot over medium heat with no oil for 10 minutes, stirring, until they release their water and soften.
Add the spiced clarified butter, garlic and ginger and cook for 5 minutes until the onions turn golden and jammy.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste, add a splash of water and cook for 10 minutes over low heat until the sauce deepens in colour.
Add the chicken and 500 ml water, then stir to coat. Cover and simmer over low heat for 40 minutes, turning the pieces occasionally.
Meanwhile, boil the eggs for 10 minutes, cool, peel and prick lightly with a fork. Add them to the stew for the last 10 minutes.
Season with the remaining salt and serve with injera.
tips: Patience with the onions is the secret. They should almost melt into the sauce.
Doro wat tastes even better the next day.
photo: A deep red-brown, glossy chicken stew with drumsticks and halved boiled eggs nestled in the sauce, served on a large round injera-lined platter with rolled injera on the side.

name: Zigni (Spiced Beef Stew)
description: A fiery Eritrean beef stew in a thick berbere and tomato sauce, slow-cooked until the meat is meltingly tender.
steps: Finely chop the onions and cook them in a large heavy pot over medium heat for 10 minutes with no oil, stirring, until soft and reduced.
Add the vegetable oil, garlic and ginger and cook for 3 minutes.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste and cook gently for 5 minutes, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Add the beef, salt and 600 ml water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer over low heat for 1 hour 30 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beef is very tender.
Boil the eggs for 10 minutes, peel them and add them to the pot for the last 10 minutes.
Stir in the spiced clarified butter, cook uncovered for 5 minutes until the sauce is thick and oily, and serve with injera.
tips: Use a cheaper cut like shin or chuck. It becomes tender and keeps its flavour.
Reduce the berbere to 2 tablespoons for a milder stew.
photo: A bowl of dark red, thick beef stew with tender chunks of meat and halved eggs, glistening with spiced butter, set on injera with extra rolled injera beside it.

name: Egusi Soup
description: A thick, nutty Nigerian soup of ground melon seeds, palm oil, leafy greens and tender beef, traditionally eaten with pounded yam or eba.
steps: Place the beef in a pot with half the chopped onion, the stock cube, a little salt and 700 ml water. Cook over medium heat for 35 minutes until nearly tender, then keep the stock.
Blend the peppers and the remaining onion into a coarse puree.
Heat the palm oil in a wide pot over medium heat for 2 minutes, then add the pepper puree and fry for 10 minutes until the water has cooked off and the oil rises.
Mix the ground egusi with 4 tablespoons of water into a thick paste and drop spoonfuls into the oil. Do not stir; let them cook for 5 minutes until they form soft curds, then fold gently.
Add the beef with about 400 ml of its stock, the crayfish and the cleaned smoked fish. Simmer on low heat for 10 minutes.
Stir in the chopped spinach and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until just wilted. Taste, adjust the salt and serve hot with pounded yam, eba or rice.
tips: Let the egusi form curds before stirring. That is what gives the classic lumpy texture.
Washed, chopped bitter leaf or pumpkin leaves work in place of spinach.
photo: A deep bowl of golden-orange egusi soup with soft curds, dark green leaves and chunks of beef, glistening with palm oil, next to a smooth mound of pounded yam.

name: Suya (Spiced Beef Skewers)
description: Thinly sliced beef coated in smoky, peanut-based yaji spice and grilled until charred, the famous Nigerian street food.
steps: Grind the roasted peanuts in a food processor or blender to a coarse powder, being careful not to turn them into butter.
Mix the ground peanuts with the ginger, garlic powder, onion powder, smoked paprika, cayenne, crumbled stock cube and salt. This is your yaji spice.
Place the beef slices in a bowl, pour on the oil and rub in two-thirds of the yaji spice until every slice is coated. Marinate for at least 30 minutes.
Thread the beef onto skewers, folding the slices over as you go. If using wooden skewers, soak them in water first.
Heat a grill, griddle pan or barbecue to high and cook the skewers for 3 to 4 minutes per side until browned with charred edges.
Sprinkle the skewers with the remaining yaji and serve with sliced raw onion and tomato.
tips: Slice the beef very thinly. Partially freezing it for 30 minutes makes this easier.
Do not overcook the meat or it turns dry.
photo: Charred beef skewers dusted generously with rust-red yaji spice on a wooden board, served with raw red onion rings and sliced tomato on a piece of paper.

name: Thieboudienne (Fish & Rice)
description: Senegal's national dish: whole-spice stuffed fish simmered with vegetables in tomato broth, then rice cooked in the same flavourful liquid.
ingredients: white fish steaks (cod or sea bream)
steps: Make the stuffing by blitzing the parsley, 4 garlic cloves, half the scotch bonnet, half an onion, salt and black pepper into a coarse paste. Cut slits in the fish and press the paste in. Marinate for 30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and fry the fish for 3 minutes per side until lightly golden. Remove and set aside.
In the same oil, fry the remaining sliced onion for 5 minutes, then add the tomato paste and cook for 5 minutes, stirring.

Add 1.5 litres water, crumbled stock cube, tamarind and the whole carrots, cassava and aubergine cut in large chunks. Simmer over medium heat for 20 minutes, then add the cabbage wedges and cook 10 minutes more until all vegetables are tender.
Return the fish to the pot for the last 8 minutes of cooking, then carefully lift the fish and vegetables out onto a plate and keep warm.
Rinse the rice, add it to the strained broth (about 700 ml, topping up with water if needed) and bring to the boil.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes until the rice is tender and a little crusty at the bottom. Serve the rice on a platter topped with the fish and vegetables.
tips: The crispy rice at the bottom of the pot, called xonoos, is considered the best part.
Soak the rice in warm water for 10 minutes first if you are using regular long grain.
photo: A large round platter of orange-red rice topped with golden fried fish steaks, wedges of cabbage, carrot, cassava and aubergine, with a lime wedge and fresh parsley.

name: Chicken Yassa
description: Chicken marinated in lemon, mustard and a mountain of onions, grilled then braised in the sweet-sharp onion sauce and served over rice.
steps: Slice the onions into thin half-moons. Mix them in a large bowl with the lemon juice, mustard, crushed garlic, chopped chilli, black pepper, salt and 2 tablespoons of oil.
Add the chicken and turn to coat. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 4 hours, or overnight.
Lift the chicken out of the marinade, keeping the onions. Grill under a hot grill or on a barbecue for 6 to 8 minutes per side until browned and charred in places.
Heat the remaining oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the marinated onions and bay leaves and cook for 15 minutes, stirring, until soft and sweet.
Add 150 ml water and the browned chicken. Cover and simmer over low heat for 30 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce is thick.
Stir in the olives and cook for 3 minutes. Serve hot over white rice.
tips: The long marinade is what makes yassa. Do not rush it.
Add a little more lemon at the end if you like a sharper sauce.
photo: Charred chicken legs resting on a bed of glossy golden caramelised onions with green olives, spooned over white rice on a deep serving dish.

name: Mafe (Peanut Stew)
description: A velvety West African stew of beef and root vegetables in a rich peanut and tomato sauce, served over steamed rice.
steps: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef in batches for 6 to 8 minutes, then set aside.
In the same pot, cook the sliced onions for 6 minutes until golden, then add the garlic and tomato paste and cook 3 minutes.
Return the beef, add the crumbled stock cube, whole scotch bonnet and 1 litre of water. Bring to the boil, cover and simmer over low heat for 45 minutes.
Whisk the peanut butter with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it back into the pot.
Add the sweet potato, carrots and cabbage in big chunks. Simmer uncovered over medium-low heat for 25 minutes until the vegetables are tender and the oil from the peanut butter rises to the surface.
Remove the scotch bonnet, season with salt and serve over rice. Cook the rice according to its packet while the stew simmers.
tips: Leave the scotch bonnet whole for flavour without too much heat, and burst it only if you like it hot.
Use unsweetened peanut butter only.
photo: A bowl of thick, creamy orange-brown peanut stew with chunks of beef, sweet potato and carrot, served beside a mound of white rice and finished with a drizzle of the red oil.

name: Swahili Pilau
description: The aromatic spiced rice of the Kenyan coast, cooked with beef in pilau masala, caramelised onions and potatoes.
steps: Boil the beef in 500 ml water with the salt, half the garlic and half the ginger over medium heat for 40 minutes, until nearly tender. Drain, saving the stock.
Rinse the rice and soak in water for 15 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat, add the cumin seeds and cinnamon stick for 30 seconds, then add the sliced onions and cook for 15 minutes until deep golden brown.
Add the remaining garlic and ginger, the chopped tomatoes and pilau masala, and cook for 5 minutes until the tomatoes collapse.
Add the beef and quartered potatoes and stir for 3 minutes.
Add the drained rice and about 650 ml of the beef stock (top up with water). Bring to the boil, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes.
Rest for 10 minutes without lifting the lid, then fluff the rice with a fork and serve with kachumbari (tomato and onion salad).
tips: Dark caramelised onions give pilau its brown colour. Do not rush them.
Make your own pilau masala by grinding cumin, cardamom, cloves, black peppercorns and cinnamon.
photo: A shallow dish of brown, fluffy spiced rice with tender beef pieces and potato chunks, garnished with fried onions and served with a small bowl of fresh tomato and onion kachumbari.

name: Samaki wa Kupaka (Coconut Fish Curry)
description: Grilled fish smothered in a tangy, creamy coconut and tamarind sauce, a signature dish of the Swahili coast.
steps: Rub the fish with the lemon juice, half the turmeric, half the cumin, half the garlic and salt. Leave for 15 minutes.
Grill or pan-fry the fish in 2 tablespoons of oil over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side until golden and just cooked. Set aside.
In a wide pan, heat the remaining oil over medium heat and cook the finely chopped onion for 5 minutes until soft.
Add the remaining garlic, grated ginger, turmeric, cumin and the sliced chilli, and cook for 1 minute.
Pour in the coconut milk and tamarind paste, stir and simmer gently for 8 minutes until slightly thickened.
Slide the fish into the sauce and spoon the sauce over for 3 minutes. Sprinkle with fresh coriander and serve with rice or chapati.
tips: Do not boil the coconut sauce hard or it may split.
Squeeze extra lemon over the finished dish for brightness.
photo: Golden grilled fish fillets in a creamy, yellow-orange coconut sauce speckled with green coriander, served in a shallow dish next to white rice.

name: Sambusa
description: Crisp triangular pastries filled with spiced minced beef, onion and herbs, a must-have at Ramadan iftar tables. Makes about 18.
steps: Cook the minced beef in a dry pan over medium-high heat for 8 minutes, breaking it up, until browned and any liquid has evaporated.
Add the finely chopped onion, garlic and chilli, then cook for 5 minutes. Stir in the cumin, coriander, turmeric and salt and cook for 2 minutes.
Remove from the heat, stir in the chopped fresh coriander and spring onions, and let the filling cool completely.
Mix the flour and water into a thin paste for sealing.

Cut each pastry sheet into strips about 8 cm wide. Put a spoonful of filling at one end of a strip and fold the corner over it to form a triangle, then keep folding the strip along its length like a flag. Seal the end with the flour paste.
Heat the oil in a deep pan over medium heat to about 170C. Fry the sambusas in batches for 2 to 3 minutes per side until golden brown and crisp.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve hot with lemon wedges or chilli sauce.
tips: The filling must be fully cool and dry or the pastry will go soggy.
Freeze uncooked sambusas on a tray, then fry straight from the freezer.
photo: A pile of crisp golden triangular sambusas on a plate lined with paper, one broken open to show the spiced beef filling, with lemon wedges and a small bowl of green chilli sauce.

name: Kelewele (Spiced Plantain)
description: Cubes of ripe plantain tossed in ginger, chilli and spices then fried until sticky and caramelised, Ghana's favourite street snack.
steps: Peel the plantains and cut them into 2 cm cubes.
Grate the ginger and garlic, then mix them in a bowl with the cayenne, ground cloves, nutmeg and salt.
Add the plantain cubes and toss until every piece is coated. Rest for 10 minutes.
Heat the oil in a deep pan over medium heat to about 170C.
Fry the plantain in two batches for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until the edges are dark golden and caramelised.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve warm with roasted peanuts.
tips: Use very ripe plantains with lots of black spots for sweetness.
Do not crowd the pan or the plantain steams instead of frying.
photo: Golden-brown caramelised plantain cubes dusted with spice, heaped in a small bowl or paper cone, with a handful of roasted peanuts beside them.

name: Mandazi
description: Lightly sweet, cardamom-scented East African doughnuts, fried until puffed and golden, perfect with chai. Makes about 16 pieces, serving 8.
steps: In a large bowl, mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, cardamom, salt and desiccated coconut.
Rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs.
Beat the egg with the milk and add to the dry ingredients, mixing to form a soft dough. Knead for 3 minutes until smooth.
Cover and rest the dough for 20 minutes.
Roll out the dough to about 1 cm thick and cut into triangles or diamonds with a knife.
Heat the oil in a deep pan over medium heat to about 170C. Fry the mandazi in batches for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until puffed and golden brown.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve warm or at room temperature.
tips: If the oil is too hot they brown outside while staying raw in the centre.
Mandazi keep for two days in an airtight tin.
photo: A pile of golden-brown triangular mandazi, lightly puffed and glistening, on a woven plate with a cup of milky chai beside them.

name: Puff-Puff
description: Soft, chewy, golden balls of sweetened yeast dough deep-fried until puffed, Nigeria's favourite party snack. Makes about 24 balls.
steps: In a large bowl, mix the flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg and salt.
Gradually pour in the warm water, whisking by hand for 2 to 3 minutes into a thick, smooth, stretchy batter.
Cover the bowl with a towel and leave in a warm place for 1 hour until doubled in size and full of bubbles.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pan over medium heat to about 170C. Stir the batter gently once.
Scoop a small handful of batter, squeeze it through your fist or use a spoon and drop balls the size of a golf ball into the oil. Fry in batches without crowding.
Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, turning often, until deep golden brown all over.
Remove with a slotted spoon, drain on kitchen paper and serve warm.
tips: Keep the oil at medium heat so the inside cooks through before the outside darkens.
Dust with extra sugar or cinnamon sugar while still warm if you like.
photo: A pile of round, golden-brown puff-puff with a slightly rough, glistening surface on a plain white plate, one torn open to show the soft airy centre.
